description: Test your knowledge of PA G3 | Hemodynamic Disorders covering Starling forces, oedema pathogenesis, and fluid classification.

cards.text: Write the formula for net filtration pressure. Which Starling forces favour filtration and which favour reabsorption?
cards.answer: Net filtration pressure = (Pc − Pi) − (πc − πi). Pc and πi favour filtration (outward); Pi and πc favour reabsorption (inward).

tip.tip: Pc and πi push OUT; Pi and πc pull IN — subscripts encode the direction.

cards.text: What are the normal values for capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc) at the arteriolar and venular ends? What physiological consequence follows?
cards.answer: ~32 mmHg at arteriolar end; ~12 mmHg at venular end. Filtration predominates at arteriolar end, reabsorption at venular end.

tip.tip: Arteries high (32), veins low (12) — pressure drop drives the filtration-reabsorption switch.

cards.text: Name two clinical conditions causing oedema via increased capillary hydrostatic pressure. What type of oedema results?
cards.answer: Right-heart failure (venous back-pressure) and venous obstruction (DVT, portal hypertension). Results in dependent, pitting oedema.

tip.tip: CHF + DVT = high pressure shoves fluid OUT → dependent pitting oedema.

cards.text: Define kwashiorkor and explain its oedema pathophysiology. Name two characteristic clinical signs.
cards.answer: Protein-energy malnutrition with adequate calories but severe protein deficiency causing hypoalbuminaemia → loss of plasma oncotic pressure → pitting oedema. Classic signs: moon face and pot-belly.

tip.tip: Moon face + pot-belly + protein deficit = kwashiorkor — the swollen facial appearance is iconic.

cards.text: What is filariasis, which organism causes it, and what oedema syndrome results?
cards.answer: Infection by Wuchereria bancrofti (mosquito-borne nematode) causing chronic obliterative lymphangitis → lymphatic obstruction. Results in elephantiasis: massive, non-pitting oedema of lower limbs, scrotum, or vulva.

tip.tip: Filaria BLOCKS lymphatics → MASSIVE non-pitting oedema; the name 'elephantiasis' mirrors the grotesque limb enlargement.

cards.text: Compare protein content and pathogenic mechanism of transudate vs exudate.
cards.answer: Transudate: <3 g/dL protein, hydrostatic/oncotic imbalance (CHF, nephrotic). Exudate: >3 g/dL protein, inflammatory vascular permeability (pneumonia, PE, TB).

tip.tip: Trans = Thin protein (mechanical imbalance); Ex = eXcess protein (inflammation).

cards.text: State the purpose of Light's criteria and name the three parameters assessed.
cards.answer: Classifies pleural effusions as transudate or exudate using: (1) protein ratio (fluid/serum), (2) LDH ratio (fluid/serum), (3) absolute LDH in fluid. ≥1 criterion met = exudate.

tip.tip: Light's Protein-LDH rule: if ANY one parameter exceeds cutoff → call it exudate (OR logic, not AND).

cards.text: List the five pathogenic categories of oedema formation with one clinical example each.
cards.answer: (1) Increased hydrostatic pressure (CHF), (2) Decreased plasma oncotic pressure (nephrotic syndrome), (3) Lymphatic obstruction (filariasis), (4) Sodium and water retention (renal failure), (5) Increased vascular permeability (inflammation/sepsis).

tip.tip: HOP-SP: Hydrostatic, Oncotic, Lymphatic obstruction, Sodium-water retention, Permeability — the five mechanisms of all oedema.
